claim: Mitochondrial division is essential for survival in mammals.
source: Mitochondrial division is a complex process that is essential for survival in mammals (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012; Archer, 2014) and is facilitated by the actin cytoskeleton (De Vos et al., 2005; DuBoff et al., 2012; Korobova et al., 2013, 2014; Hatch et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012 and Archer, 2014

claim: Mitochondrial division is facilitated by the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Mitochondrial division is a complex process that is essential for survival in mammals (Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012; Archer, 2014) and is facilitated by the actin cytoskeleton (De Vos et al., 2005; DuBoff et al., 2012; Korobova et al., 2013, 2014; Hatch et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including De Vos et al., 2005; DuBoff et al., 2012; Korobova et al., 2013, 2014; Hatch et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015

claim: Two distinct steps define mitochondrial division: an initial constriction of mitochondrial membranes, followed by final membrane scission.
source: Two distinct steps define mitochondrial division - an initial constriction of mitochondrial membranes, followed by final membrane scission (Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013; Korobova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013; Korobova et al., 2014

claim: Scission is mediated by the dynamin-related protein, Drp1, which self-assembles on the surface of the mitochondrial outer membrane into helices that drive final mitochondrial division.
source: Scission is mediated by the dynamin-related protein, Drp1, which self-assembles on the surface of the mitochondrial outer membrane into helices that drive final mitochondrial division (Lackner and Nunnari, 2009; Archer, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lackner and Nunnari, 2009 and Archer, 2014

claim: The initial constriction step narrows the mitochondrial tube diameter, which is necessary for Drp1 helix assembly.
source: The initial constriction step narrows the mitochondrial tube diameter, which is necessary for Drp1 helix assembly (Labrousse et al., 1999; Yoon et al., 2001; Legesse-Miller et al., 2003; Ingerman et al., 2005; Friedman et al., 2011; Mears et al., 2011; Murley et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Labrousse et al., 1999; Yoon et al., 2001; Legesse-Miller et al., 2003; Ingerman et al., 2005; Friedman et al., 2011; Mears et al., 2011; Murley et al., 2013

claim: The initial constriction step is independent of Drp1.
source: This step is independent of Drp1 and occurs at ER-mitochondria intersection zones where ER tubules associate with and wrap around the mitochondrial outer membrane along the plane of mitochondrial division (Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013; Korobova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013; Korobova et al., 2014

claim: The initial constriction step occurs at ER-mitochondria intersection zones where ER tubules associate with and wrap around the mitochondrial outer membrane along the plane of mitochondrial division.
source: This step is independent of Drp1 and occurs at ER-mitochondria intersection zones where ER tubules associate with and wrap around the mitochondrial outer membrane along the plane of mitochondrial division (Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013; Korobova et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013; Korobova et al., 2014

claim: Along ER-mitochondria intersection zones, actin filaments polymerize, providing the force needed for constriction that floppy ER tubules lack.
source: Along these zones, actin filaments polymerize, providing the force needed for constriction that floppy ER tubules lack (Korobova et al., 2013, 2014; Hatch et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korobova et al., 2013, 2014 and Hatch et al., 2014

claim: Inverted formin 2 (INF2) is a formin family protein that promotes actin filament polymerization in a regulated fashion.
source: Inverted formin 2 (INF2) is a formin family protein that promotes actin filament polymerization in a regulated fashion (Korobova et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korobova et al., 2013, 2014

claim: An ER-anchored splice isoform of INF2 (INF2-CAAX) has been shown to facilitate mitochondrial constriction and division via its actin polymerization activity.
source: An ER-anchored splice isoform of INF2 (usually referred to as INF2-CAAX) (Chhabra et al., 2009; Korobova et al., 2013) has been shown to facilitate mitochondrial constriction and division via its actin polymerization activity (Korobova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chhabra et al., 2009 and Korobova et al., 2013

claim: Spire proteins are membrane-binding actin-nucleators that interact with and regulate formin proteins.
source: Spire proteins are membrane-binding actin-nucleators that interact with and regulate formin proteins (Bosch et al., 2007; Quinlan et al., 2007; Pechlivanis et al., 2009; Kerkhoff, 2011; Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Zeth et al., 2011; Quinlan, 2013; Montaville et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Bosch et al., 2007; Quinlan et al., 2007; Pechlivanis et al., 2009; Kerkhoff, 2011; Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Zeth et al., 2011; Quinlan, 2013; Montaville et al., 2014

claim: Synergistic promotion of actin assembly by Spire and formin proteins has been implicated in driving a variety of processes ranging from vesicle trafficking to DNA repair in the nucleus.
source: Synergistic promotion of actin assembly by Spire and formin proteins has been implicated in driving a variety of processes ranging from vesicle trafficking to DNA repair in the nucleus (Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011; Montaville et al., 2014; Belin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011; Montaville et al., 2014; Belin et al., 2015

claim: Vertebrates have two known Spire genes, Spire1 and Spire2.
source: Vertebrates have two known Spire genes, Spire1 and Spire2.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Each Spire protein contains four actin-monomer binding WH2 domains necessary for nucleating actin filaments.
source: Each Spire protein contains highly conserved domains with specific capabilities, including: four actin-monomer binding WH2 domains necessary for nucleating actin filaments; an mFYVE domain that binds to intracellular membranes and facilitates oligomerization (Kerkhoff, 2011; Dietrich et al., 2013); and an N-terminal KIND domain that serves to bind to and regulate formin proteins (Bosch et al., 2007; Quinlan et al., 2007; Pechlivanis et al., 2009; Kerkhoff, 2011; Pfender et al., 2011; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Zeth et al., 2011; Quinlan, 2013; Montaville et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Spire protein structure

claim: Each Spire protein contains an mFYVE domain that binds to intracellular membranes and facilitates oligomerization.
source: Each Spire protein contains highly conserved domains with specific capabilities, including: four actin-monomer binding WH2 domains necessary for nucleating actin filaments; an mFYVE domain that binds to intracellular membranes and facilitates oligomerization (Kerkhoff, 2011; Dietrich et al., 2013); and an N-terminal KIND domain that serves to bind to and regulate formin proteins (Bosch et al., 2007; Quinlan et al., 2007; Pechlivanis et al., 2009; Kerkhoff, 2011; Pfender et al., 2011; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Zeth et al., 2011; Quinlan, 2013; Montaville et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerkhoff, 2011 and Dietrich et al., 2013

claim: Each Spire protein contains an N-terminal KIND domain that serves to bind to and regulate formin proteins.
source: Each Spire protein contains highly conserved domains with specific capabilities, including: four actin-monomer binding WH2 domains necessary for nucleating actin filaments; an mFYVE domain that binds to intracellular membranes and facilitates oligomerization (Kerkhoff, 2011; Dietrich et al., 2013); and an N-terminal KIND domain that serves to bind to and regulate formin proteins (Bosch et al., 2007; Quinlan et al., 2007; Pechlivanis et al., 2009; Kerkhoff, 2011; Pfender et al., 2011; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Zeth et al., 2011; Quinlan, 2013; Montaville et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Bosch et al., 2007; Quinlan et al., 2007; Pechlivanis et al., 2009; Kerkhoff, 2011; Pfender et al., 2011; Vizcarra et al., 2011; Zeth et al., 2011; Quinlan, 2013; Montaville et al., 2014

claim: No Spire proteins have been shown previously to localize to mitochondria or the ER.
source: Although no Spire proteins have been shown previously to localize to mitochondria or the ER (Dietrich et al., 2013), here we report a previously uncharacterized alternate splice-isoform of Spire1 (named Spire1C) that localizes to mitochondria, promotes actin assembly on mitochondrial surfaces, and interacts with ER-anchored INF2 to regulate mitochondrial constriction and division.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2013

claim: Spire1C is a previously uncharacterized alternate splice-isoform of Spire1 that localizes to mitochondria.
source: Although no Spire proteins have been shown previously to localize to mitochondria or the ER (Dietrich et al., 2013), here we report a previously uncharacterized alternate splice-isoform of Spire1 (named Spire1C) that localizes to mitochondria, promotes actin assembly on mitochondrial surfaces, and interacts with ER-anchored INF2 to regulate mitochondrial constriction and division.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Spire1C promotes actin assembly on mitochondrial surfaces.
source: Although no Spire proteins have been shown previously to localize to mitochondria or the ER (Dietrich et al., 2013), here we report a previously uncharacterized alternate splice-isoform of Spire1 (named Spire1C) that localizes to mitochondria, promotes actin assembly on mitochondrial surfaces, and interacts with ER-anchored INF2 to regulate mitochondrial constriction and division.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Spire1C interacts with ER-anchored INF2 to regulate mitochondrial constriction and division.
source: Although no Spire proteins have been shown previously to localize to mitochondria or the ER (Dietrich et al., 2013), here we report a previously uncharacterized alternate splice-isoform of Spire1 (named Spire1C) that localizes to mitochondria, promotes actin assembly on mitochondrial surfaces, and interacts with ER-anchored INF2 to regulate mitochondrial constriction and division.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Spire1C contains a previously uncharacterized unique 58 amino acid alternate exon sequence (ExonC).
source: We identified and characterized a novel alternate splice-isoform of Spire1 that contains KIND and WH2 domains common to all Spire proteins, as well as a previously uncharacterized unique 58 amino acid alternate exon sequence (ExonC) (Figure 1A and see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3 for details on Spire1C cloning, probe generation, and sequence information).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures

claim: Spire1C mRNA is present in multiple mouse tissues.
source: After determining that Spire1C mRNA was present in multiple mouse tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), we examined its presence and conservation among species.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: ExonC is highly conserved among mammalian species including rat, rabbit, human, dog, elephant, opossum, and platypus.
source: When compared to mouse, we found striking identity in ExonC for rat, rabbit, human, dog, elephant, opossum, platypus, and chicken.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis using the UCSC Genome Browser

claim: Human ExonC differs from mouse ExonC by 2 residues (96% identical).
source: Compared to our amplified mouse sequence of 58 amino acids, human ExonC differs by 2 residues (96% identical), platypus by 8 residues (86% identical), and chicken by 12 residues (79% identical).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison data

claim: Platypus ExonC differs from mouse ExonC by 8 residues (86% identical).
source: Compared to our amplified mouse sequence of 58 amino acids, human ExonC differs by 2 residues (96% identical), platypus by 8 residues (86% identical), and chicken by 12 residues (79% identical).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison data

claim: Chicken ExonC differs from mouse ExonC by 12 residues (79% identical).
source: Compared to our amplified mouse sequence of 58 amino acids, human ExonC differs by 2 residues (96% identical), platypus by 8 residues (86% identical), and chicken by 12 residues (79% identical).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison data

claim: ExonC is not found in the annotated zebrafish sequence.
source: It is not found in the annotated zebrafish sequence.
evidence: Based on sequence database analysis

claim: Conservation among species extends beyond the coding exon and into the upstream and downstream intronic regions of the gene, stretching ∼150 bases in the 3′ direction.
source: Conservation among species extends beyond the coding exon and into the upstream and downstream intronic regions of the gene, stretching ∼150 bases in the 3′ direction (data not shown).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis data

claim: The conserved extensions surrounding ExonC are likely involved in splicing regulation of the exon.
source: These conserved extensions are likely involved in splicing regulation of the exon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of conserved intronic regions

claim: The high level of conservation within and surrounding ExonC suggests that its role is indispensible for the health of the organism.
source: The high level of conservation within and surrounding ExonC suggests that its role is indispensible for the health of the organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high degree of sequence conservation observed

claim: Myc-Spire1C shows robust localization to mitochondria when cotransfected with mitoRFP in U2OS cells.
source: myc-Spire1C: U2OS cells cotransfected with myc-Spire1C and mitoRFP show robust localization of myc-Spire1C to mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Endogenous Spire1C labeled with an antibody raised against ExonC (α-ExonC) shows mitochondrial localization in U2OS cells.
source: α-ExonC: U2OS cells stained with an antibody raised against ExonC (α-ExonC) and expressing mitoRFP show endogenous Spire1C labeling on mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B

claim: GFP-ExonC shows robust targeting to mitochondria when cotransfected with mitoRFP in U2OS cells.
source: GFP-ExonC: U2OS cells cotransfected with GFP-ExonC and mitoRFP show robust targeting of GFP-ExonC to mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Myc-Spire1ΔC shows no specific targeting to mitochondria when cotransfected with mitoRFP in U2OS cells.
source: myc-Spire1ΔC: U2OS cells cotransfected with myc-Spire1ΔC and mitoRFP show no specific targeting of myc-Spire1ΔC to mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B

claim: ExonC is necessary and sufficient for localization to mitochondria.
source: Testing the role of ExonC in mitochondrial targeting of Spire1C, we found that a GFP-tagged ExonC fusion protein robustly localized to mitochondria in expressing cells (Figure 1B, GFP-ExonC). By contrast, a myc-tagged Spire1C construct lacking ExonC never showed specific mitochondrial localization (Figure 1B, myc-Spire1ΔC). These results suggest that Spire1C is an endogenously expressed mitochondria-associated protein that targets to mitochondria via its ExonC domain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating that ExonC alone is sufficient for mitochondrial targeting and its deletion abolishes targeting

claim: GFP-ExonC labeling on mitochondria surrounds that of mitoRFP labeling.
source: GFP-ExonC labeling on mitochondria surrounded that of mitoRFP labeling (Figure 2A), suggesting Spire1C localizes to the periphery of mitochondria, most likely on the mitochondrial outer membrane.
evidence: Supported by structured illumination microscopy (SIM) data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Spire1C localizes to the periphery of mitochondria, most likely on the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: GFP-ExonC labeling on mitochondria surrounded that of mitoRFP labeling (Figure 2A), suggesting Spire1C localizes to the periphery of mitochondria, most likely on the mitochondrial outer membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on SIM imaging data showing peripheral localization relative to the mitochondrial matrix marker

claim: In cells cotransfected with OMI-mCherry and GFP-Spire1C, the N-terminal GFP tag is mostly depleted within 60 s after trypsin treatment in the fluorescence protease protection assay.
source: Cells cotransfected with OMI-mCherry and GFP-Spire1C (N-terminal GFP tag, left) or GFP-ExonC (N-terminal GFP-tag, middle) were treated with 20 μM digitonin and 4 mM trypsin. In both cases OMI-mCherry fluorescence remained, whereas the N-terminal GFP tags were mostly depleted within 60 s after trypsin treatment.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence protease protection assay data shown in Figure 2D and Videos 1-3

claim: In cells cotransfected with OMI-mCherry and GFP-ExonC, the N-terminal GFP tag is mostly depleted within 60 s after trypsin treatment in the fluorescence protease protection assay.
source: Cells cotransfected with OMI-mCherry and GFP-Spire1C (N-terminal GFP tag, left) or GFP-ExonC (N-terminal GFP-tag, middle) were treated with 20 μM digitonin and 4 mM trypsin. In both cases OMI-mCherry fluorescence remained, whereas the N-terminal GFP tags were mostly depleted within 60 s after trypsin treatment.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence protease protection assay data shown in Figure 2D and Videos 1-3

claim: In cells transfected with ExonC-GFP (C-terminus GFP tag), GFP fluorescence remains unchanged after 60 s of trypsin treatment in the fluorescence protease protection assay.
source: In contrast, in cells transfected with ExonC-GFP (C-terminus GFP tag), GFP fluorescence remains unchanged after 60 s of trypsin treatment.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence protease protection assay data shown in Figure 2D and Videos 1-3

claim: The WH2 and KIND domains of Spire1C face the cytoplasm.
source: These results suggest that the WH2 and KIND domains of Spire1C face the cytoplasm (since both reside N-terminal to ExonC) (Figure 2C), a topology where they could participate in formin-binding and actin-nucleation activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence protease protection assay results showing that N-terminal tags are accessible to trypsin

claim: The C-terminus of ExonC is not exposed to the cytoplasm.
source: The data further suggest that the C-terminus of ExonC is not exposed to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence protease protection assay results showing that C-terminal tags are protected from trypsin

claim: ExonC may be embedded in the outer membrane, either as a transmembrane or hairpin protein.
source: This raises the possibility that ExonC is embedded in the outer membrane, either as a transmembrane or hairpin protein.
evidence: This is speculation based on the topology data from the fluorescence protease protection assay

claim: Transmembrane domain prediction software indicates that residues 26–46 within ExonC form an α-helix characteristic of prokaryotic transmembrane domains.
source: In support of this notion, transmembrane domain prediction software (Claros and von Heijne, 1994) indicated that residues 26–46 within ExonC form an α-helix characteristic of prokaryotic transmembrane domains.
evidence: Based on computational prediction using transmembrane domain prediction software

claim: Secondary structure prediction software PHYRE predicted a second α-helix within ExonC.
source: Secondary structure prediction software PHYRE (Kelley and Sternberg, 2009) also predicted a second α-helix within ExonC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on computational prediction using PHYRE software, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Full-length Spire1C with GFP fused to the C-terminus (Spire1C-GFP) remains mostly cytoplasmic and no longer properly localizes to mitochondria.
source: Interestingly, when we expressed a full-length Spire1C construct with GFP fused to the C-terminus (Spire1C-GFP), the protein remained mostly cytoplasmic and no longer properly localized to mitochondria (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental observation of Spire1C-GFP localization

claim: Spire1C is a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, possibly with a hairpin conformation.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that Spire1C is a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, possibly with a hairpin conformation given ExonC's two predicted α-helix domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence including topology data, computational predictions, and the effect of C-terminal tagging

claim: Photobleaching of a portion of a mitochondrial element expressing GFP-Spire1C results in rapid recovery of fluorescence, with replenishment arising first in regions close to the bleach site and later at regions further away.
source: Photobleaching of a portion of a mitochondrial element that expressed GFP-Spire1C resulted in rapid recovery of fluorescence, with replenishment arising first in regions close to the bleach site and later at regions further away (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), similar to that seen for GFP-tagged proteins that feely diffuse along membranes (Cole et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by photobleaching experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Very little fluorescence recovery occurs when an entire mitochondrial element expressing GFP-Spire1C is photobleached during the same time period as partial bleaching.
source: In contrast, very little recovery during the same time period occurred when an entire mitochondrial element expressing GFP-Spire1C was photobleached (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by photobleaching experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Spire1C diffuses laterally along mitochondrial membranes, rather than rapidly binding and dissociating from the membrane.
source: Thus, Spire1C appears to diffuse laterally along mitochondrial membranes, rather than rapidly bind and dissociate from the membrane, further supporting the idea of Spire1C being a mitochondrial outer membrane protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the photobleaching recovery patterns observed

claim: In non-transfected cells, only low levels of actin co-localized with mitochondria, without any apparent specificity.
source: In non-transfected cells, only low levels of actin co-localized with mitochondria, without any apparent specificity (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, control).
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Upon Spire1C overexpression, actin accumulated to high levels specifically on mitochondria.
source: Upon Spire1C overexpression, however, actin accumulated to high levels specifically on mitochondria (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Spire1C overexpression).
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Actin enrichment on mitochondrial surfaces upon Spire1C overexpression is not dependent on Spire's formin-binding KIND domain.
source: This actin enrichment on mitochondrial surfaces was not dependent on Spire's formin-binding KIND domain, since overexpression of Spire1C lacking the KIND domain (Spire1CΔKIND) still induced actin enrichment on mitochondrial surfaces (Figure 3, Spire1CΔKIND overexpression).
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3

claim: Actin enrichment on mitochondria is muted upon overexpression of Spire1C mWH2, which contains mutations in its WH2 domains that block Spire-mediated actin nucleation.
source: In contrast, actin enrichment on mitochondria was muted upon overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Spire1C mWH2 overexpression), which contains mutations in its WH2 domains that block Spire-mediated actin nucleation (Loomis et al., 2006; Salles et al., 2009) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Spire1C promotes actin assembly on mitochondria through Spire1C's ability to nucleate actin filaments.
source: These results demonstrated that Spire1C promotes actin assembly on mitochondria, most likely through Spire1C's ability to nucleate actin filaments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that actin accumulation depends on functional WH2 domains but not the KIND domain

claim: Overexpression of Spire1C results in a significant shift towards fragmented mitochondria compared to control cells.
source: While all cells in all conditions in this study displayed a combination of fragmented and tubular mitochondria, overexpression of Spire1C resulted in a significant shift towards fragmented mitochondria compared to control cells (Figure 4A, +Spire1C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 results in a shift towards tubular mitochondria.
source: In contrast, overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 or Spire1CΔKIND resulted in a shift towards tubular mitochondria (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Overexpression of Spire1CΔKIND results in a shift towards tubular mitochondria.
source: In contrast, overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 or Spire1CΔKIND resulted in a shift towards tubular mitochondria (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Depletion of Spire1C using shRNA results in a shift towards tubular mitochondria.
source: Depletion of Spire1C using shRNA also resulted in a shift towards tubular mitochondria (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Spire1C overexpression results in shorter mitochondria on average (2.2 ± 0.5 μm).
source: U2OS cells overexpressing Spire1C display shorter mitochondria (second panel, 2.2 ± 0.5 μm, nmitochondria = 211, ncells = 14, p < 0.0001)
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and 4C

claim: Overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 results in longer mitochondria (6.2 ± 1.52 μm) compared to control cells (3.57 ± 0.45 μm).
source: whereas cells overexpressing Spire1C mWH2 (third panel, 6.2 ± 1.52 μm, nmitochondria = 332, ncells = 15, p < 0.0001) or Spire1CΔKIND (fourth panel, 9.0 ± 1.50 μm, nmitochondria = 232, ncells = 16, p < 0.0001) display longer, more tubulated mitochondria compared to control cells (first panel, 3.57 ± 0.45 μm, nmitochondria = 322, ncells = 34).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and 4C

claim: Overexpression of Spire1CΔKIND results in longer mitochondria (9.0 ± 1.50 μm) compared to control cells (3.57 ± 0.45 μm).
source: whereas cells overexpressing Spire1C mWH2 (third panel, 6.2 ± 1.52 μm, nmitochondria = 332, ncells = 15, p < 0.0001) or Spire1CΔKIND (fourth panel, 9.0 ± 1.50 μm, nmitochondria = 232, ncells = 16, p < 0.0001) display longer, more tubulated mitochondria compared to control cells (first panel, 3.57 ± 0.45 μm, nmitochondria = 322, ncells = 34).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4A and 4C

claim: Spire1C knockdown results in longer mitochondria (6.1 ± 1.26 μm).
source: Cells cotransfected with Spire1 shRNA and mitoEmerald with no detectable α-ExonC labeling (lower row) display long, tubulated mitochondria (6.1 ± 1.26 μm, nmitochondria = 222, ncells = 17).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and 4C

claim: Spire1C overexpression increases the frequency of mitochondrial fission events.
source: We found that fission events increased in frequency when cells were overexpressing Spire1C, whereas overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 or Spire1CΔKIND decreased the frequency of fission events (Figure 4C, right graph).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data quantified in Figure 4C

claim: Overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 decreases the frequency of mitochondrial fission events.
source: We found that fission events increased in frequency when cells were overexpressing Spire1C, whereas overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 or Spire1CΔKIND decreased the frequency of fission events (Figure 4C, right graph).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data quantified in Figure 4C

claim: Overexpression of Spire1CΔKIND decreases the frequency of mitochondrial fission events.
source: We found that fission events increased in frequency when cells were overexpressing Spire1C, whereas overexpression of Spire1C mWH2 or Spire1CΔKIND decreased the frequency of fission events (Figure 4C, right graph).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data quantified in Figure 4C

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of Spire1C decreases the frequency of mitochondrial fission events.
source: Similarly, shRNA-mediated knockdown of Spire1C decreased the frequency of fission events (Figure 4C, right graph).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data quantified in Figure 4C

claim: Spire1C promotes mitochondrial fission via Spire1C's actin-nucleating and formin-binding capabilities.
source: Taken together, our results show Spire1C promotes mitochondrial fission via Spire1C's actin-nucleating and formin-binding capabilities.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data showing that both WH2 and KIND domains are required for Spire1C to promote mitochondrial fission

claim: Upon overexpression of Spire1C or Spire1C mWH2, there is no significant change in ER-mitochondrial overlap or crossover sites compared to control cells.
source: Upon overexpression of Spire1C or Spire1C mWH2, we observed no significant change in ER-mitochondrial overlap or crossover sites of ER tubules and mitochondria compared to control cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and 5B

claim: In cells overexpressing Spire1CΔKIND, there is a significant decrease in ER-mitochondria overlap.
source: However, in cells overexpressing Spire1CΔKIND, we observed a significant decrease in ER-mitochondria overlap, as well as a decrease in the number of ER tubules crossing over mitochondria (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and 5B

claim: In cells overexpressing Spire1CΔKIND, there is a decrease in the number of ER tubules crossing over mitochondria.
source: However, in cells overexpressing Spire1CΔKIND, we observed a significant decrease in ER-mitochondria overlap, as well as a decrease in the number of ER tubules crossing over mitochondria (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and 5B

claim: The KIND domain of Spire1C plays a role in regulating the extent of ER-mitochondria intersections within cells.
source: This suggested that the KIND domain of Spire1C might play a role in regulating the extent of ER-mitochondria intersections within cells, and that Spire1CΔKIND-mediated disruption of mitochondrial fission (see Figure 4C, right panel) could be due to a reduction in ER-mediated mitochondrial constriction in these cells (Friedman et al., 2011; Korobova et al., 2013; Murley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Spire1CΔKIND reduces ER-mitochondria contacts

claim: The C-terminal half of INF2 (INF2-CT), but not the N-terminal half (INF2-NT), associates with a GST-tagged Spire1C KIND domain in GST pull-down assays.
source: We found that the C-terminal half of INF2 (INF2-CT), but not the N-terminal half (INF2-NT), associated with a GST-tagged Spire1C KIND domain, but not GST alone (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Addition of the N-terminal half of INF2 (INF2-NT) inhibits the interaction between Spire1C KIND and INF2-CT in GST pulldown assays.
source: Addition of the N-terminal half of INF2 (INF2-NT) inhibited the interaction between Spire1C KIND and INF2-CT in our GST pulldown assays (Figure 6A; last well), suggesting that INF2's ability to self-interact (Chhabra and Higgs, 2006; Ramabhadran et al., 2012, 2013) can regulate its association with Spire1C.
evidence: Supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6A

Here, we demonstrate that Spire1C, a novel mitochondrial outer membrane protein, can serve this role by both binding to INF2 as well as by acting as an actin-nucleator.

claim: The establishment of Spire1C as a mitochondrial outer membrane protein suggests that Spire1C is optimally positioned to serve as a molecular hub that links mitochondrial dynamics to the actin cytoskeleton as well as to the ER.

evidence: This is an inference based on Spire1C's localization and its ability to interact with both actin and INF2

claim: There are important functions for actin in mitochondrial dynamics, such as mitochondrial motility in neurons.

evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies
